item.title: Creating Became Cheaper. They Started Paying for Something Else
item.description:
Recent interviews have made me think about how the value of technical expertise is changing in the job market. I'm not talking about AI starting to write code instead of developers – enough has been said about that. I'm more interested in something else: if technical implementation is becoming more accessible, what exactly does a company want from a person hired for a leadership position? One of the recent conversations was about the position of CTO in a large company. The second was about a new project in fintech that required a manager. The project was to be launched, developers were already in place, but processes needed to be built from scratch. In both cases, the task was not just to manage development. It was necessary to form a working environment around oneself, grow a team, organize people's interaction, and ensure that all this worked as a single system. I have been developing for a long time, and for the last eight years, I have been a manager. Almost a year ago, I left employment to understand new AI tools and test them on my own engineering experience. During this time, I created several tools for my tasks. I didn't prepare software specifically for interviews. On the contrary, I made it because I myself lacked a convenient and sufficiently rigorous development process with AI. But something unexpected happened during the interviews: talking about my experience took a few minutes, and then we moved on to the software I wrote, and we could discuss it for another half an hour. Why is that? Read more

item.title: Why LLMs Ignore System Prompts: Dialogue History is Stronger Than Instructions
item.description:
A familiar situation: the system prompt clearly states what the model absolutely must not do, yet it does it anyway. You rewrite the rule, add "IMPORTANT," caps, and examples; it gets slightly better, then reverts. Eventually, you start suspecting the model, its settings (like temperature), or the provider. We encountered this in a voice assistant and investigated thoroughly: replaying battle queries and changing one factor at a time. The prompt was irrelevant. The model followed its own dialogue history, and below I'll show how we discovered this, the resulting metrics, and what to do if you're building an LLM chatbot, agent, or assistant. Read on.

item.title: Four Protocols and One "Allow" Button: How I Connected Claude Code, Codex, Qwen, and Hermes to Telegram
item.description:
Claude Code and Codex can work for a long time unsupervised, but only while you're sitting next to them. An agent might ask for permission to execute a command or pose a clarifying question, waiting for your response. Step away from your computer, and everything grinds to a halt. I once had to leave urgently for business, and I had a lot of tasks for the day. I wanted to assign them to agents from my phone and confirm commands with a button press, rather than keeping six terminals open. This led to the creation of agent-hub: a desktop application in Rust where each Telegram group thread is a separate agent session on my computer. During a 3-4 hour trip, I processed over six tasks through it. Similar solutions exist, but they didn't suit me. It's important for me that each task has its own conversation history and that I don't have to remember session IDs, and group threads are perfect for this. In this article, I'll focus less on the tool itself and more on its internal workings: how four agents with different protocols are unified under a single interface, how a permission request turns into a Telegram button and back, and what Telegram limitations had to be circumvented. Read on.

item.title: I asked AI to teach me to communicate directly with hardware
item.description:
I wanted to remove all layers of abstraction between myself and the computer. To leave my intention, AI, and the bytes that the processor executes. In the process, programs for RISC-V and ARM64 appeared, a flash drive with its own UEFI application, a physical Dell, colored objects on the screen, and a cat to which a new world can be transferred via Bluetooth. Not all layers disappeared. But it became clearer what exactly they do and how much work they usually do for us. Read more

item.title: Linear Attention Can Do More
item.description:
Hello, Habr! We are students from the AI Services and Platforms workshop at the Higher School of Economics' Engineering and Mathematics School and VK: Pavel Alekseev, Alexander Rozhkin, Andrey Argatkin, Alexey Pavlov, and Matvey Kamenev. In this project, we investigated how to improve the quality of models with linear attention to the level of ordinary transformers. Such a mechanism allows processing long sequences without a quadratic increase in computational costs, making it promising for more economical training of language models and processing long documents. During autoregressive text generation, it helps save memory: instead of a growing KV-cache, a fixed-size state can be stored. The starting point was the Dense Attention architecture, which uses simple matrix operations without softmax but shows high quality in published experiments. Our supervisor, Andrey Argatkin, set a new research direction in the article on Dense Attention. We will explore which model components provide this result and whether they can be transferred to other attention variants. The working hypothesis is that linear models lag in quality not only due to the replacement of softmax but also due to architectural settings and training. The number of heads, positional encoding, and layer scheme chosen for standard transformers are not necessarily optimal for a linear mechanism. We tested whether changing these components and MLM pre-training would reduce the quality gap without reverting to global softmax attention. Read more

item.title: [Translation] Automating My 35mm Film Scanning Process
item.description:
I love photography. There's something thrilling about looking through the lens, composing a shot, and working on the resulting photo. I've gone through DSLRs and mirrorless cameras until I finally fell in love with the Canon AE-1P, an analog SLR my father used to travel the world with before settling in the US. Shooting film is simple yet specific: reflected light hits plastic film, burning a chemical image into it. The combination of lighting, film type, and lens creates magically unique compositions. For years, my workflow looked like this: load film, take photos, send film to the lab, wait for development, pick up film, cut negatives into strips, insert them into a holder, scan each frame with a special scanner, open each file in Darktable, manually invert, make edits, and then decide where to store and/or publish the exported image. At first, this process seemed delightful, but the more film I shot, the more time it took to process all 36 frames. Read more

item.title: Shaky Trust: Human Perception of AI "Consciousness" and "Awareness"
item.description:
In today's world, AI products are everywhere, from amusing AI-generated content to AI assisting in tasks like choosing products, conducting interviews, and summarizing research. This ubiquitous AI raises questions about trust. A comprehensive study by the University of Munich found that trust in AI remains low, even when its behavior mimics humans. This article delves into how AI attempted to imitate human creation in the study, what gave it away, and why people remain distrustful of entities that pose no existential threat. The findings are detailed in the researchers' report.

item.title: [Translation] The Decoherence Trap
item.description:
In this essay, I introduce the concept of decoherence, which is the accumulation of models in a system that are individually workable but incompatible with each other or redundant. In such a system, the main cost of changes falls on reconciling these models and preventing unintended side effects. In other words, it's what happens when a low-quality mess drowns out a useful signal in a vast sea of noise. Read more

item.title: What to Check Before Implementing an AI Agent in a Corporate Environment
item.description:
The word "incident" is increasingly appearing alongside "agent" in news feeds, but we're not here to discourage you from implementing agent applications in corporate processes. Quite the opposite. This article is about how to avoid ending up in the news headlines with the word "incident" and about ten practical questions to ask before a pilot. Read more

item.title: Eight AI agents and five ways to know what they are doing: how we connected OpenCode, Kilo, and Pi to the Mac notch
item.description:
Lumio is a free app for the MacBook notch. It shows what your AI agents are currently doing: who is working, who has finished, who is waiting for command permission. You can grant permission directly from the notch, without switching to the terminal. There's also a pixel office where each session is a person at their desk. Until today, Lumio understood Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Antigravity. In version 1.3, OpenCode, Kilo Code, and Pi were added. It might seem like just three more lines in the settings. In reality, it's three different ways to connect and a week of work, two days of which were spent not on code, but on testing it with real agents without paid keys. Read more

item.title: Cyber-Marxism, or Why AI is Incompatible with Capitalism, and Why We Face a Collapse of the Socio-Economic Formation
item.description:
The article discusses the incompatibility of Artificial Intelligence with capitalism, arguing that AI's advancement will lead to the collapse of the current socio-economic system. It contrasts the optimistic views of AI proponents with the author's belief that AI will disrupt labor markets, devalue traditional assets, and necessitate a fundamental shift in economic structures, potentially leading to communism or a world dominated by AI agents. The author also touches upon the generational conflict and the increasing disconnect between technological progress and human life cycles as contributing factors to societal instability.

item.title: Analyst Career Growth: How to Reach the Next Level and What Changes with AI
item.description:
Hello, Habr! This is Anna Kudelina, Deputy Technical Director for Analytics at RT Labs. Five years ago, I wrote an article on how to prepare for a system analyst interview. It was very popular, with 130,000 readers and 263 saves, and was published in professional communities. Several people later told me the article helped them become analysts or advance their careers. I realized that sharing my accumulated experience on career growth is valuable, so I decided to write a follow-up. In my 6 years at RT Labs, I've climbed the ladder from a junior system analyst to leading the company's entire analytics function. My tasks, responsibilities, and way of thinking have evolved. Through my own experience, I now know the hidden pitfalls that cause people to get stuck. While my first article was about how to become an analyst, this one is about what to do next. Read on.
